The fact that he made use of sinful means in order to make more sure of securing the end desired, namely, of the false pretence that he had been directed by an angel to do this, may be explained, as Hengstenberg suggests (<hi type="italic">Dissert</hi>. vol. ii. p. 149), on the ground that when Jeroboam introduced his innovations, he had sinned by keeping silence, and that the appearance of the Judaean prophet had brought him to a consciousness of this sin, so that he had been seized with shame on account of his fall, and was anxious to restore himself to honour in his own eyes and those of others by intercourse with this witness to the truth. But however little the lie itself can be excused or justified, we must not attribute to him alone the consequences by which the lie was followed in the case of the Judaean prophet. For whilst he chose reprehensible means of accomplishing what appeared to be a good end, namely, to raise himself again by intercourse with a true prophet, and had no wish to injure the other in any way, the Judaean prophet allowed himself to be seduced to a transgression of the clear and definite prohibition of God simply by the sensual desire for bodily invigoration by meat and drink, and had failed to consider that the divine revelation which he had received could not be repealed by a pretended revelation from an angel, because the word of God does not contradict itself. He was therefore obliged to listen to a true revelation from God from the moth of the man whose pretended revelation from an angel he had too carelessly believed, namely, to the announcement of punishment for his disobedience towards the commandment of God, which punishment he immediately afterwards endured, “for the destruction of the flesh, but for the preservation of the spirit: 1Co 15:5” (<hi type="italic">Berleb. Bible</hi>). That the punishment fell upon him alone and not upon the old prophet of Bethel also, and that for apparently a smaller crime, may be accounted for “not so much from the fact that the old prophet had lied with a good intention (this might hold good of the other also), as from the fact that it was needful to deal strictly with the man who had just received a great and holy commission from the Lord” (O. v. Gerlach). It is true that no bodily punishment fell upon the old prophet, but this punishment he received instead, that with his lie he was put to shame, and that his conscience must have accused him of having occasioned the death of the man of God from Judah. He was thereby to be cured of his weakness, that he might give honour to the truth of the testimony of God. “Thus did the wondrous providence of God know how to direct all things most gloriously, so that the bodily destruction of the one contributed to the spiritual and eternal preservation of the soul of the other” (<hi type="italic">Berleb. Bible</hi>). - Concerning the design of these marvellous events, H. Witsius has the following remarks in his <hi type="italic">Miscell. ss</hi>. i. p. 118 (ed. nov. 1736): “So many wondrous events all occurring in one result caused the prophecy against the altar at Bethel to be preserved in the mouths and memories of all, and the mission of this prophet to become far more illustrious. Thus, although the falsehood of the old man of Bethel brought disgrace upon himself, it injured no one but the man of God whose credulity was too great; and, under the overruling providence of God, it contributed in the most signal manner to the confirmation and publication of the truth.”<note placement="foot">Compare with this the remark of Theodoret in his <hi type="italic">quaest</hi>. <hi type="italic">43 in 3 libr. Reb</hi>.: “In my opinion this punishment served to confirm the declaration concerning the altar. For it was not possible for the statement of such a man to be concealed: and this was sufficient to fill with terror those who heard it; for if partaking of food contrary to the command of God, and that not of his own accord, but under a deception, brought such retribution upon a righteous man, to what punishments would they be exposed who had forsaken the God who made them, and worshipped the likenesses of irrational creatures?”</note> <div eID="gen4959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4960" type="x-p"/> The heaping up of the marvellous corresponded to the great object of the mission of the man of God out of Judah, through which the Lord would enter an energetic protest against the idolatrous worship of Jeroboam at its first introduction, to guard those who feared God in Israel, of whom there were not a few (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.16">2Ch 11:16</reference>; 2Ki 18:3; 2Ki 19:18), from falling away from Him by joining in the worship of the calves, and to take away every excuse from the ungodly who participated therein.
entries.c78116f8ec2a883b936e5f35ccf3e874e3455601: 1Ki 13:33 <div eID="gen4960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4961" type="x-p"/> But this did not lead Jeroboam to conversion. He turned not from his evil way, but continued to make high priests from the mass of the people. ויּעשׂ ויּשׁב, “he returned and made,” i.e., he made again or continued to make. For the fact itself compare 1Ki 12:31. “Whoever had pleasure (החפץ, cf., Ges. §109), he filled his hand, that he might become a priest of the high places.” מלּא את־ידו, to fill the hand, is the technical expression for investing with the priesthood, according to the rite prescribed for the consecration of the priests, namely, to place sacrificial gifts in the hands of the persons to be consecrated (see at <reference osisRef="Lev.7.37">Lev 7:37</reference> and Lev 8:25.). The plural בּמות כּהני is used with indefinite generality: that he might be ranked among the priests of high places.
entries.a17a9674423282db6656afb8d9d1389db157fbfe: 1Ki 13:34 “And it became in (with) this thing the sin of the house of Jeroboam, and the destroying and cutting off from the earth;” that is to say, this obstinate persistence in ungodly conduct was the guilt which had as its natural consequence the destroying of his house from the face of the earth. הזּה בּדּבר is not a mistake for הזּה הדּבר, but בּ is used, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.33">1Ch 9:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.7.23">1Ch 7:23</reference>, to express the idea of being and persisting in a thing (for this use of בּ compare Ewald, §295, f.). Reign of Jeroboam. - Vv. 1-18. <hi type="italic">Ahijah’s prophecy against Jeroboam and the kingdom of Israel</hi>. - As Jeroboam did not desist from his idolatry notwithstanding the threatened punishment, the Lord visited him with the illness of his son, and directed the prophet Ahijah, to whom his wife had gone to ask counsel concerning the result of the illness, to predict to him not only the cutting off of his house and the death of his sick son, but also the thrusting away of Israel out of the land of its fathers beyond the Euphrates, and in confirmation of this threat caused the sick son to die when the returning mother crossed the threshold of her house again.  <chapter eID="1Kgs.13"/> <div eID="gen4961" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p>AND behold, there came a man of God <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">An Holy Prophet.</ns0:note> out of Judah by the word of the LORD <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">By Divine Inspiration and Command.</ns0:note> unto Bethel: and Jeroboam stood by the altar to <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="2">2 And he cried against the altar <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">And consequently, against all that Worship; which is oft signified by the name of the <ns0:hi>altar.</ns0:hi> See <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 19. 19. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 9. 13. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 7. 13. and 13. 10.</ns0:note> in the word of the LORD, and said, O altar, altar <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He directs his Speech to the Altar; partly, because the following signs were wrought upon it; and partly to signifie, That <ns0:hi>Ieroboam</ns0:hi> would no more regard his words, than the Altar did; and yet they should take effect.</ns0:note>, thus saith the LORD, Behold, a child <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">

For this was in it self uncer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tain, and wholly depended upon Man's Will, both as to the having of a Child, and as to the giving it this Name. There<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore God can certainly, and effectually over-rule Man's Will which way he pleaseth; or else it was possible, that this Prediction should have been false; which is Blasphemous to imagine.</ns0:note>, and up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on thee shall he offer the priests <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Synecdochically, the Bones of the Priests, 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 23. 15, 16. whereby the Altar should be defiled.</ns0:note> of the high<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />places that burn incense upon thee, and mens bones shall be burnt upon thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And he gave a sign the same day <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He then wrought a Miracle, to assure them of the Truth of his Prophecy.</ns0:note>, saying, This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the sign which the LORD hath spoken: Behold, the altar shall be rent, and the ashes that <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> upon it poured out.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And it came to pass when king Jeroboam heard the saying of the man of God, which had cryed against the altar in Bethel, that he put forth his hand <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">To point out the Man whom he would have the Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple lay hands on, and to stir them up to do so.</ns0:note> from the altar <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Where it was imployed, in offering something upon it.</ns0:note>, saying, Lay hold on him. And his hand which he put forth against him, dried up <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Or, withered,</ns0:hi> the Muscles and Sinews, the instruments of Moti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, were shrunk up. This God did, partly to chastise <ns0:hi>Ie<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />roboam</ns0:hi> for offering violence to the Lord's Prophet: partly, to secure the Prophet against further Violence: and partly, that in this Example God might shew, how highly he re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sents the injuries done to his Ministers, in, and for the faith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful discharge of their Office.</ns0:note>, so that he could not pull it in again to him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 The altar also was rent, and the ashes pou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />red out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given by the word of the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And the king answered <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Spoke; as that Word is oft used in both Testaments.</ns0:note>, and said unto the man of God, Intreat now the face of the LORD thy God <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Who by his Zeal for thee, hath manifested himself to be thy God and Friend, in a singular manner; and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore will hear thy Prayers for me, though he will not re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gard mine, because I have forsaken him and his Worship.</ns0:note>, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored me again. And the man of God be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sought <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> of the LORD<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> the LORD <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To assure <ns0:hi>Ieroboam,</ns0:hi> that what he had said, was not from ill-will to him, and that he heartily desired his Reformation, not his Ruine.</ns0:note>, and the kings hand was re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stored again <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Partly to assure him, that the stroke was from God: partly, because he Repented of that Violence which he intended against the Prophet, for which God in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />flicted it: and partly, that this goodness of God to him, might have led him to Repentance; or, if he continued Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />penitent, leave him without all excuse.</ns0:note>, and became as <ns0:hi>it was</ns0:hi> before.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 And the king said unto the man of God, Come home with me, and refresh thy self, and I will give thee a reward <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Horrid Stupidity!                   <ns0:p n="9">9 For so was it charged me by the word of the LORD <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">My refusal of thy favour, is not from any contempt, or hatred of thy Person; but in obedience to the just Command of my God, who hath forbidden me all further Converse or Communication with thee.</ns0:note>, saying, Eat no bread, nor drink water <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">To wit, in that place, or with that People. Whereby God declares, how detestable they were in Gods Eyes; not because their Idolatry was so bad as that of the <ns0:hi>Heathens,</ns0:hi> but because they were vile Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />states from the True God, and embraced this Idol-worship, against the light of their own Consciences, meerly to com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ply with the Kings humour and command: and because their vicinity and Relation to the Tribe of <ns0:hi>Iudah,</ns0:hi> made this more dangerous, as to their infection by it.</ns0:note>, nor turn again by the same way that thou camest <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">That by thy avoiding the way that led thee to <ns0:hi>Bethel</ns0:hi> as execrable, al<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />though thou wentest by my special Command, thou might<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est teach all others, how much they should abhor that way, and all thoughts of going to that place, or to such people, upon any trivial and unnecessary occasion.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 So he went another way, and returned not by the way that he came to Bethel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 ¶ Now there dwelt an old prophet <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">A Prophet of the Lord; one to whom, and by whom, God did sometimes impart his mind; as is manifest from <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 20, 21. and one that had a respect to the Lords holy Prophets, and gave credit to their Predictions: all which the following Relation shews: but whether he was an holy and good Man, may justly be doubted, seeing all those qua<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lifications might meet in a vicious man, to, and by whom he may Reveal some part of his Mind, as he did to <ns0:hi>Balaam, Numb.</ns0:hi> 23. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and in such, his other qualities are sometimes found; and we find him in a downright and premeditated Lye, and that without any great temptation to it, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 18. And albeit, an holy Prophet might possibly have continued in the Kingdom of Israel, he would never have gone from his own habitation, to dwell at <ns0:hi>Bethel,</ns0:hi> the chief Seat of Ido<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />latry, unless with design to Preach against it: which it is evident he did not; his Sons seem to have been present at, and to have joyned with others in that Idolatrous worship, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. and that not without their Fathers connivence.</ns0:note> in Be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thel <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">For thither he came to dwell, probably expecting some great ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vantages from <ns0:hi>Ieroboam;</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>he came out of Samaria,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 23. 18. where he either was born, and had lived be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore.                   <ns0:p n="13">13 And he said unto his sons, Saddle me the ass. So they sadled him the ass, and he rode thereon:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And went after the man of God, and found him sitting under an oak <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Being faint and weary with his journey, and possibly with the heat, which makes him chuse this shady place; and especially with hunger and thirst, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 9. And he might ea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sily guess that this was the old Prophet, by his age and car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riage, and, it may be, by his Prophetical Mantle, and by the Character which his Sons had given him.</ns0:note>: and he said unto him, <ns0:hi>Art</ns0:hi> thou the man of God that camest from Judah? And he said, I <ns0:hi>am.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 Then he said unto him, Come home with me, and eat bread.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And he said, I <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In <ns0:hi>Bethel,</ns0:hi> where thou desirest me to do it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 For <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a word <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> it was said to me by the word of the LORD, Thou shalt eat no bread, nor drink water there, nor turn again to go by the way that thou camest.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 He said unto him, I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> a prophet also as thou <ns0:hi>art,</ns0:hi> and an angel spake unto me by the word of the LORD, saying, Bring him back with thee into thine house, that he may eat bread, and drink water. <ns0:hi>But</ns0:hi> he lied unto him <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Not with evil design against him, but out of curiosity, to know all the truth and circumstances from his own mouth, and to express his kindness to him, and to relieve his pressing hunger; whereby possibly he thought to please God, and to compensate for his miscarriages. But his sin was great; for he did not onely tell a premeditated lye, but also made God a lyar, and to contradict himself, and all this without any pretence of necessity, or benefit to himself.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 So he went back with him, and did eat bread in his house, and drank water.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 ¶ And it came to pass, as they sat at the table <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">There the Prophet meets with a severe Judgment, where he was pleasing himself with this seasonable refreshment.</ns0:note>, that the word of the LORD came <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">By secret instinct into his mind; as sometimes God spake to <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> and other Prophets when they were in company, with others.</ns0:note> unto the prophet that brought him back <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">So he makes this Prophet publickly to call him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self lyar, and to pronounce a terrible Sentence against him, to whom he professed so much kindness. Indeed the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> words are ambiguous, and by others rendred thus, <ns0:hi>to the Prophet whom he had brought back;</ns0:hi> which agrees very well with the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Phrase; and may seem to be the best Translation, by comparing <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 23. where the very same Phrase i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> so rendred; and <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 26. where this message is said to be <ns0:hi>spoken to him.</ns0:hi> But these Arguments are not cogent; not that from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 23. because it is a common thing for the same Phrase in divers Verses, and sometimes in one and the same Verse, to be diversly used: nor that from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 27. for that may be rendred <ns0:hi>concerning him.</ns0:hi> And Therefore our Trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lation is better, as is manifest from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 21.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And he cried <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">With a loud Voice, the effect of his passion, both for his own guilt and shame, and for the Prophets approaching <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>sery, and his unhappy influence both in procuring and i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> denouncing of it.</ns0:note> unto the man of God that came from Judah, saying, Thus saith the LORD, Forasmuch as thou hast disobeyed the mouth <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">

                  <ns0:p n="22">22 But camest back, and hast eaten bread, and drunk water in the place, of the which <ns0:hi>the LORD</ns0:hi> did say to thee, Eat no bread, and drink no water; thy carcase shall not come unto the sepulchre of thy fathers <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thou shalt not die a natural, but a violent death; and that in this journey, before thou returnest to thy native habitatition; and thy Carkass shall not be buried in the pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />per Sepulchre; which was esteemed a kind of Curse, and a note of Infamy; as the contrary was reckoned an honour and blessing. See <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 14. 13. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 14. 19, 20. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 22. 19. and 26. 24.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 ¶ And it came to pass, after he had eaten bread, and after he had drunk, that he sadled for him the ass <ns0:note place="bottom">That he might sooner come to his home, and, if possi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble, escape the Judgment threatned. But, it is observable, he doth not accompany him; his guilty Conscience making him to expect and fear to be involved in the same Judgment with him.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>to wit,</ns0:hi> for the prophet whom he had brought back.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 And when he was gone, a <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 20. 36.</ns0:note> lion met him <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">For there were many Lions in <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> and this was brought hither by Gods special Providence.</ns0:note> by the way, and slew him <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Why doth God punish a good man so severely for so small an offence? <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> First, His sin was not small, for it was a gross diso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bedience to a positive command. <ns0:hi>Obj.</ns0:hi> But he supposed, and was told by another Prophet, that God had repealed his command, and so was deceived. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> He had no sufficient discharge from the former command; for he neither was assured that the old man was a Prophet, nor that the message he delivered was from God; but had reason to suspect the contrary, or at least to enquire the mind of God in this doubtful point, which he grosly neglected to do, and wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lingly believed the message, because it suited with his own inclination and necessity. Add to this, that he being a Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet was obliged to the greater exactness in obedience to all Gods Precepts; and therefore this sin was much greater in him than in another, because hereby God was dishonoured, and the Authority and Success of his message blasted, and <ns0:hi>Ieroboam</ns0:hi> and the Idolatrous <ns0:hi>Israelites</ns0:hi> hardened in their wicked courses; for the prevention whereof it was necessa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry that God should exercise severity towards him. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />condly, As his sin was not so small, so his punishment was not so great, as may be imagined. For as to his outward man, his Bodily death (which was a Debt that he owed to God and Nature) in this way was not so painful and terri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble as many other kinds of death; and as to his Soul, God, by giving him a Gracious admonition both of his sin and danger, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 21, 22. awakened him to true Repentance, which doubtless he practised, and so was prepared for his death, and by this sudden death freed from all the miseries of an evil time and world, and speedily let in to Eternal Glory. <ns0:hi>Ans.</ns0:hi> Thirdly, As the world and all men in it were made for Gods Glory, and all their Lives and Deaths ought to be laid out in his Service; so it cannot seem strange nor harsh if God should bring his deserved Death upon him in this manner, for the accomplishment of his own Glorious Designs, as to vindicate his own Honour and Justice from the imputation of partiality; to assure the Truth of his Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dictions, and thereby provoke <ns0:hi>Ieroboam</ns0:hi> and his Idolatrous followers to Repentance; to justify himself in all his Dread<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful Judgments which he intended to inflict upon <ns0:hi>Ieroboam</ns0:hi>'s House, and the whole Kingdom of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> for their Cursed Apostacy; and to warn all succeeding sinners not rashly to venture upon small sins, and especially to take heed of great<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />er sins, for which they might expect far sorer punishments.</ns0:note>: and his carcase <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> cast in the way <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">His Life and Soul being gone, his Dead Body falls to the ground, and lies there.</ns0:note>, and the ass stood by it: the lion also stood by the carcase <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">See on <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 28.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:289" />27 And he spake to his sons, saying, Saddle me the ass <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Being secure as to himself, because so many others had been there without any harm; and because he perceived the Prophet's Death was a Judgment of God, and that for spe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cial reasons.</ns0:note>. And they saddled <ns0:hi>him.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And he went and found his carcase cast in the way, and the ass, and the lion standing by the carcase: the lion had not eaten the carcase, nor <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> broken.</ns0:note> torn the ass <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Here was a concurrence of Miracles; That the Ass did not run away from the Lion, according to his nature and cu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stom, but boldly stood still, as reserving himself for the carry<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of the Prophet to his Burial; that the Lion did not de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vour its prey, as the manner is; nor yet go away when he had done his work which he was sent for, but stood still, partly, to preserve the Carkass of the Prophet from other wild Beasts or Fowls, which would quickly have eaten it; partly, as an evidence that the Prophet's Death was not casual, nor the effect of a Lions hungry and ravenous di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sposition, but of Gods singular and just Judgment; and consequently, that his Prediction was Divine, and should be infallibly accomplished in its proper time; and part<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, as a token of Gods favour to the deceased Prophet, of whose very Carkass he took such special care: thereby sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifying, that although for Wise and Just reasons he thought fit to take away his life, yet his remains were precious to him, and his Soul did live in his sight.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 And the prophet took up the carcase of the man of God, and laid it upon the ass, and brought it back: and the old prophet came to the city, to mourn, and to bury him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And he laid his carcase in his own grave <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">So that threatning, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. was fulfilled; and withal, the memory of his Prophecy was revived and preserved among them, and his very Carkass resting there, might be a witness of their madness and desperate wickedness, in continuing in their abominable Idolatry, after such an assurance of the dreadful effects of it.</ns0:note>, and they <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">The old Prophet and his Sons, and others, whom common humanity taught to lament the un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />timely death of so worthy a Person.</ns0:note> mourned over him, <ns0:hi>saying,</ns0:hi> Alas my bro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Which was an usu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />al form of expression in Funeral-lamentations. See <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 22. 18.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And it came to pass after he had buried him, that he spake to his sons, saying, When I am dead, then bury me in the sepulchre wherein the man of God <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> buried, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="32">32 For the saying which he cried by the word of the LORD, against the altar in Bethel, and a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst all the houses of the high places, which <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> in the cities of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See Chap. 16. 24.</ns0:note> Samaria <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of the Kingdom of <ns0:hi>Samaria;</ns0:hi> as it was called, though not when this Fact was done, yet before these Books were written. <ns0:hi>Samaria</ns0:hi> was properly the name of one City, 1 <ns0:hi>King:</ns0:hi> 20. 1. but from hence the whole Kingdom of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> was so called, <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 31 5. <ns0:hi>Hos:</ns0:hi> 7. 1. and 8. 5. and <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 3. 9. and the King of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> is called <ns0:hi>the King of Samaria,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 1. 3. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 10. 7. and (as here) we read of <ns0:hi>the cities of Samaria, Ezra</ns0:hi> 4. 10.</ns0:note>, shall surely come to pass.</ns0:p>

                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> After all these things: the Singular Number put for the Plural; after so many, and evident, and successive Miracles. Which is noted to aggravate his Infidelity and Apostacy.</ns0:note> Jeroboam returned not from his evil way, but <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">

                  <ns0:p n="34">34 And this thing became sin <ns0:note place="bottom">Either, an occasion of sin, and means of hardening all his Posterity in their Idolatry: or, <ns0:hi>a punishment,</ns0:hi> for so the word <ns0:hi>sin</ns0:hi> is oft used.
